title: The delusion of a particle-only universe
subtitle: The world is more than its building blocks
author: David Yates
introduction: If everything that happens in the world ultimately comes down to the behavior of fundamental particles, it would seem that other entities, from cells to human beings, from currencies to financial markets, aren't really causing anything at all—that they are just shadows cast by patterns at the most fundamental level. But philosopher David Yates argues this conclusion is wrong. The whole affects the parts, and higher-level structures don't just describe what is happening at lower levels in more convenient terms—they actively shape what is possible. This means that chemists, biologists, psychologists, and economists aren't chasing shadows. They are studying structures that genuinely shape how the world unfolds.
body:
In 1974, Jerry Fodor published a seminal paper titled ‘Special Sciences’, in which he argued for an intuitive and compelling picture of the relationship between fundamental physics and higher-level sciences such as biology, psychology and economics. Our world, according to Fodor, is arranged hierarchically, with fundamental physical particles at the bottom, combining to form molecules, which combine to form cells, which combine to form complex organisms, some of which have mental states, among them humans, who combine to form complex societies. The sciences are likewise arranged, with physics at the bottom, followed by chemistry, biology, physiology, neuroscience, psychology, sociology and economics. Now it is vanishingly unlikely, says Fodor, that things that share e.g. psychological or economic properties, also share some property specifiable in the language of physics or other lower-level sciences. There are indefinitely many ways in which a financial transaction might be physically implemented; and what are the chances that two different people, both thinking the thought that they ought to reduce international travel due to the climate crisis, are in exactly the same brain state?

Special sciences enable us to discover distinctive higher-level laws that are typically not expressible in the languages of the sciences below. To make the point vivid, consider a very high-level science, economics, and consider the following generalization: during a recession, the banks will lower interest rates to increase public spending and stimulate the economy. Suppose it’s an economic law that decreasing interest rates causes a rise in public spending, which in turn stimulates economic growth. What does a rise in interest rates look like, at the quantum physical level? Or an increase in spending? Or economic growth? Economic events like recessions or currency transactions will not have anything at all in common at the level of quantum physics, and so economic laws are invisible at that level. It isn’t just that biologists, psychologists and economists can’t get the funding to build particle accelerators and space telescopes; even if they could, they wouldn’t have any use for such things. The events, processes and laws that interest them simply don’t belong to physics, and must be studied within their own domains, using the characteristic techniques of their particular sciences.

Even if all forces are fundamental physical forces, there is still, I claim, plenty of causal work for higher level states to do.

Compelling though Fodor’s vision may be, given some perfectly reasonable metaphysical assumptions, it’s very hard to see how it could be true. In a series of highly influential works in the 1980s and 90s, culminating in his 1998 MIT book Mind in a Physical World, Jaegwon Kim raises a series of very challenging problems for Fodor’s view. One of the main problems he raises, the causal exclusion problem, has been the focus of much of my own work. Fodor's picture is a form of non-reductive physicalism: everything that exists, at every level, is ultimately made up of fundamental physical stuff, but that doesn't mean we can simply read off what happens at higher levels from what happens at the physical level. Non-reductive physicalism holds that mental, social and financial events are ultimately made up of fundamental physical particles, but at the same time, that there are distinctive psychological, sociological and economic laws and explanations that can’t be reproduced in the language of fundamental physics. For example, all the money on planet Earth must be somehow made up of fundamental physical particles—whether it’s the coins in your pocket or the bitcoin in your crypto wallet, it’s all physically implemented, one way or another. But just looking at the quantum state of planet Earth will not tell you whether a recession is happening.

There is no question of reducing financial transactions or trains of thought to quantum physics, but any given transaction or thought process is ultimately constituted by some mind-bogglingly complex collection of quantum physical processes. Wherein lies the problem: doesn’t all the real causal work happen at the fundamental physical level? If so, then there is no causal work left for anything else to do, and what seem to be causal processes unfolding at higher levels are really, to use Kim’s memorable phrase: “like a series of shadows cast by a moving car. The moving car represents a genuine causal process, but the series of shadows it casts, however regular and law-like it may be, does not constitute a causal process,” (1998, 45).

The shadow metaphor is indeed apt: even we can treat a shadow as if it were in motion and measure its “velocity” and “acceleration” as it “moves” across a wall. We can use this information to predict where the shadow will be after a certain time has elapsed, and depending on our measurement apparatus, this may turn out to be much easier than trying to measure the genuine velocity and acceleration of the car itself. In reality, however, “the” shadow is not in motion at all. Rather, as the car moves, it casts a series of different shadows, and treating the shadow as if it were moving is a fiction. For Kim, all special science states, events, processes (at least those that do not reduce to physics) are no more than useful fictions—shadows cast by underlying physical processes, which are useful only insofar as they correlate in regular, lawful ways with real causal processes that are too complex for us to model using physics.

The idea that fundamental physical things “do all the causal work” is known as the causal closure of the physical, and it is an exceptionally widespread view amongst philosophers. If causal closure is true, then it seems that your decision to read this sentence to find out more about closure was brought about solely by fundamental forces affecting the trajectories of the particles that make up your brain.

Closure involves a rejection of the kind of emergentism defended by British Emergentists such as C. D. Broad (The Mind and its Place in Nature, Routledge 1925), who posited special configurational forces that emerge only when fundamental physical particles are combined in specific ways. This theory posits downward causation, in which higher-level structures that are made up of fundamental physical particles also play a role in determining what happens to the very particles that make them up. Broad’s position makes it easy, in principle, to make sense of Fodor’s: special sciences are autonomous from physics to the extent that they involve the study of non-physical configurational forces and the conditions under which they emerge. But Broad’s emergentism is by now almost universally rejected, not least because it posits mysterious, unexplainable forces that appear only in things of a certain level of complexity. The question now is, how do we make sense of Fodor’s picture in a world where the only forces operative are the forces of fundamental physics? If there are no configurational forces, and all complex entities are fully constituted by fundamental physical particles, then it seems that everything that happens to complex entities—every transaction, every train of thought—has a complete fundamental physical cause. My own work on this topic aims to show that this conclusion doesn’t follow. Even if all forces are fundamental physical forces, there is still, I claim, plenty of causal work for higher level states to do.

The exclusion problem has generated a huge amount of literature and there are many ways of trying to tackle it. One option is to bite the bullet and accept Kim’s conclusion: higher-level states, for instance mental states, are not genuine causes, but correlate well enough with the underlying physical processes for it to be useful, pragmatically, to describe each other in psychological terms. Or you might try to defend the view that higher-level states inherit the causal powers of their realizers from below, raising the possibility that certain effects, such as behaviours, have causes at multiple levels simultaneously: quantum physical, neuroscientific, and psychological, for instance. This latter move, in one form or another, is by far the most popular among contemporary philosophers. My own view is different. I defend an emergentist position like Broad’s, but without positing configurational forces.

SUGGESTED VIEWING Unexplained events With George Ellis, Nancy Cartwright, Tara Shears, Michael Duff

On my view, there is downward causation from higher-level states to the physical, but it does not involve generating new forces. In my article, “From Multilevel Explanation to Downward Causation” (in Levels of Explanation, eds. K. Roberton & A. Wilson, OUP 2024) I argue that there is more to causation than just the exertion of fundamental forces.

The causal interactions that matter to us involve interactions between many particles, in very complex configurations, and in such cases, the spatiotemporal patterns that the particles make determines how the multitude of active forces composes. To illustrate, consider the familiar case of two horses pulling a barge along a canal. It is natural to say that the horses jointly possess the power to pull the barge, and that each contributes by pulling it diagonally, towards the bank upon which it walks. The resulting acceleration of the barge straight along the canal depends on the spatiotemporal structure formed by the two horses and the barge. This is a very simple pattern, to be sure, but it suffices to make the general point. Higher-level geometric patterns play a fundamental role in determining how multiple forces compose on a given occasion. Now think, for example, of the structure of a molecule—we can think of this as the spatiotemporal pattern the component atoms and electrons make in relation to each other. The chemical properties of a molecule are heavily dependent on its structure, and in my view, this is a case of downward causation in which geometric patterns play a fundamental role in determining how configurations of fundamental particles behave.

And of course, the patterns don’t stop at the chemical level—there are configurations of fundamental particles, configurations of configurations, and so on all the way up.

We philosophers are notoriously prone to overgeneralization. In pre-Socratic times, the Greek philosopher Thales of Miletus, reflecting on the way water nourishes seeds, concluded that water was the origin of all things: “all is water!” he claimed. I don’t want to sound like Thales, so I don’t claim that the hierarchical structure of the natural sciences is entirely explained by the role of spatiotemporal patterns in fundamental dynamical interactions. I see it more as a proof of concept: even if the only forces in nature are those of fundamental physics, it doesn’t follow that chemists, biologists, psychologists, and the rest, are chasing shadows. If geometric structure isn’t the whole story about downward causation, then what other kinds are there?

Consider the heart and its place within the body. It’s natural to say that the heart has the power to pump blood around the body, and that it does so by beating. If a heart is temporarily removed from a body, it retains the power to beat when electrically stimulated but loses the power to pump blood around the body by doing so. This latter power is one that the heart can only possess within the body as a whole. The left heart sends oxygenated blood to the organs of the body, which return deoxygenated blood to the right heart, which sends it to the lungs for oxygenation. The operation of the circulatory system depends not only on the spatiotemporal structure of the body, but also on causal coordination between heart, blood vessels and organs. An isolated heart can only beat; to pump blood around the body by beating, a great deal of extrinsic structure is required, some of it spatiotemporal, some of it causal, some perhaps of other kinds. If structure, in this broader sense, plays a top-down role in determining what the individual organs of the body can do, then physiology need not feel threatened by the more fundamental sciences below. In my view, the correct metaphysical approach to complex entities like the body mirrors scientific practice: not reduction to physics, but multiscale modelling.

There are obvious parallels here with Aristotle, who famously held that wholes are prior to their parts, because it is only within the whole that a part can fulfil its defining function. In my most recent work on the topic, “Hylomorphism, or Something Near Enough” (Rethinking Emergence, eds. D. Yates & A. Bryant, OUP 2026) I explore the kind of hylomorphism that results from my metaphysical views about causation and levels.

The other contributors to that book are united in their belief that, when it comes to making sense of a layered world, there is something right about the spirit Broad’s emergentism, if not the letter. Perhaps closest to my own view is the contextual emergentism of Michael Silberstein. On that view, there are no intrinsic causal powers at all, and what we think of as intrinsic powers arise from a wide range of contextual constraints. I get off the bus some way before Silberstein’s stop. On my view, there are intrinsic powers, but what it is they are powers to do is often determined by the structures in which they are embedded. To the extent that special sciences are involved in the study of such structures—their nature, realization and significance—then biology, psychology and economics are not just convenient shorthand for quantum physical processes. And the heartbeats, decisions and transactions such sciences describe are every bit as real as the quantum particles that make them up.
